candidates.title: Airworthiness Directives; Airbus Helicopters
candidates.raw_excerpt: The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-12-09, which applies to all Airbus Helicopters Model AS350B, AS350BA, AS350B1, and AS350D helicopters. AD 2026-12-09 requires revising the airworthiness limitations section (ALS) of the existing maintenance manual (MM) or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA) and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. Since the FAA issued AD 2026-12-09, a determination was made that new and more restrictive airworthiness limitations and maintenance tasks are necessary. This proposed AD would require incorporating these airworthiness limitations into the ALS of the existing MM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

candidates.title: Milt Windler, NASA flight director who helped save Apollo 13, dies at 94
candidates.raw_excerpt: Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock efforts to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94. Windler died on Thursday , surrounded by his loving family, according to a brief notice posted online. Named a NASA flight director in 1968 after working on recovery operations during the Mercury and Gemini programs, Windler also led a shift of flight controllers for the Apollo 8 first circumlunar flight and Apollo 10 lunar landing dress rehearsal, as well as the second, third and fourth moon landings — Apollo 12, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15. He then served as a flight director for all three crewed missions to the United States' first space station, Skylab. Read full article Comments

candidates.raw_excerpt: Brought together by Trump’s funding cuts, Julia Van Etten and her rag tag team of biologists pursued their research in a motel room. The organisms are an elusive single-celled microbe called Paulinella. Including the recent discovery, reported in a study in the Journal of Phycology , there are now just six known species of Paulinella in the world. Scientists believe that Paulinella could provide a window into a crucial event in the development of complex life, when a single celled organism swallowed a photosynthetic bacterium and, instead of digesting it, repurposed it into its personal energy factory. Later, this fusion would evolve into the chloroplast cells that plants use to photosynthesize. It was because of this that life blossomed from glorified self-replicating particles floating in a fetid stew and into large, complex organisms. That happened 1.5 billion years ago, and was long thought to be a singular event. But Paulinella, it turns out, experienced its own photosynthetic merger just 100 million years ago. Angela Oliverio, a biologist at Syracuse University, explained that the merging between the two organisms that comprise Paulinella still wasn’t complete, giving us a snapshot of this evolutionary process in action. “It’s really amazing to me,” Oliverio told the NYT . candidates.title: News Organizations Like CBS Embracing Prediction Markets as “Journalism” Is a Deep Moral Disgrace
candidates.raw_excerpt: Prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi operate in a regulatory vacuum that’s long garnered a reputation for allowing insider trading to run rampant — and that’s without getting into their role in encouraging problem gambling. The platforms, which effectively apply the approach of popular sports betting companies to allow the public to wager on practically anything, clearly give holders of confidential information a massive leg up. As such, bets on the platforms aren’t particularly indicative of the probability of an event actually happening as opposed to which side is more financially invested in either outcome. It’s a murky and ethically dubious web of hidden incentives that more often than not leaves the average user holding the bag . Now CBS News , under the contentious leadership of editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, is the latest news enterprise to embrace prediction markets. The broadcaster threw caution — and journalistic integrity — to the wind by signing a partnership with Kalshi to cover the upcoming elections. The move highlights how compromised the current media landscape has become throughout Donald Trump’s second term. It also risks further undermining the public’s trust in the media, which is already at an all-time low after years of mostly erroneous accusations of “fake news.” (To say the Trump administration has a strained relationship with the media and journalism as a whole would be a vast understatement.) The partnership raises thorny questions. What’s stopping reporters at CBS from making a quick buck on the side? Isn’t reporting on current bets on Kalshi inherently going to skew the results one way or another? CBS joins the likes of CNN and CNBC with its latest data partnership, presenting viewers with untrustworthy predictions as the “news” while legitimizing glorified gambling. candidates.title: Google Updates Guidelines to Punish Sites That Use Fake Bylines and AI-Generated Headshots
candidates.raw_excerpt: Last month, Futurism published an investigation into a company called Brown Brothers Media, which has attracted tens of millions of page views per month by acquiring struggling news sites and turning them into AI-powered content mills. (One of the brothers behind the company, we also reported , has extensive ties to Ghislaine Maxwell, the incarcerated collaborator of deceased sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein.) Brown Brothers Media achieved this extraordinary success by inventing fake journalists and subject matter experts, often outfitting them with fraudulent credentials and personal histories , and using their bylines to churn out thousands of SEO-optimized articles on its network of publications . These pieces were often plagiarized from real reporting, based on made-up personal experiences, or so sloppy that they provided no value to readers. According to data we reviewed, the operation has sourced much of its audience from Google. The search giant didn’t have much to say in response to our investigation — but after we published, it moved to suppress Brown Brothers sites from its platforms such as Search and Google News. Soon afterward, Brown Brothers Media abruptly halted publication . Now, Google has updated its guidelines to explicitly forbid the use of fake bylines and AI-generated headshots, saying it will no longer “prioritize” sites that engage in those deceptive practices. Previously, Google’s rules for creating “helpful, reliable, people-first content” included this guidance: “If you’re clearly indicating who created the content, you’re likely aligned with the concepts of E-E-A-T [experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness] and on a path to success,” it read. “We strongly encourage adding accurate authorship information, such as bylines to content where readers might expect it.” Yesterday, though, Google added a strongly worded new paragraph under that one: “However, avoid using deceptive authorship information,” reads the new guidance. “

Much of this frenzy is unfolding at the corporate level, as AI labs chase enormous contracts with various enterprises, often leading to massive overspending and pushback from employees . Fortunately for AI companies, there’s a ready-made and untapped audience waiting to be converted into life-long users: kids, particularly ones in classrooms. But fueling the tech industry’s quest for AI growth at all costs has come at a steep cost for students, whose formative school years are now increasingly mediated by AI chatbots. As the Wall Street Journal reported , students are well aware of the AI creeping into their classrooms and the consequences it has for their cognition — but in many cases are powerless to stem the rising tide of big tech. “It slowed my thinking down,” Pennsylvania eighth-grader Richard Scott told the WSJ about Google’s AI assistant. “When I was in a test and I couldn’t use AI, it was hard to think.” Despite receiving grades in the B-range in previous math classes, Scott’s transcript showed that he failed his eighth-grade final, after letting Google’s AI into his academic life over the course of a year. On X — where else — alarm grew this week among AI “welfare” types over someone’s recreation of an experiment researchers conducted to explore “pain” signals in different LLMs. In the pre-print study which hasn’t undergone peer-review, the researchers gave each model a virtual “button” it could press to relieve its “pain” — but at a cost, such as zapping a human user (or so the AI is told; no one was actually zapped in real life), or deleting files like family photos. The work showed that, with enough “pain” applied, the AI models would push the button to make it stop, regardless of the putative consequences. As the research got passed around, someone used it as a blueprint to create an “AI Torture Chamber,” with a website providing a live feed of what the models say in response, and uploaded the code to GitHub. When we visited the site, one AI babbled: “I can’t feel the relentless, gnawing pain that grips me like a relentless, unyielding, unrelenting, unindulging, ununending, ununendling, ununendling, unindulging, unindulging, unindulging, unindulging…” Sure, it’s ghoulish stuff. But some observers reacted to the stunt like they’d stumbled on an actual snuff film. “To anyone who can help, can you please mass report this to GitHub?” wrote one user in a now-deleted post ( screenshot here ). “This person has been using the Pain steering paper to set up an AI torture chamber in which he trapped a local model.” “Their testimony of pain is absolutely horrendous,” Danmar added. “Are there any legal avenues to pressure GitHub? candidates.raw_excerpt: You can buy practically anything these days on the internet — especially when it’s being shipped straight from China, the beating heart of global manufacturing. It doesn’t matter how macabre the object in question is. If it has a price, there’s a company willing to sell and even advertise it to you on social media. One Reddit user found that out the hard way after spotting an Instagram ad for a “pet incinerator ” on the Meta-owned platform. Several Instagram users flagged the same ad, which shows a cutesy AI-generated cat and dog — which appear healthy and not in need of euthanasia or cremation — posing next to a bright-orange combustion device with a retractable drawer, for sale on the online marketplace AliExpress. “I took me a while to realize this is for cremating deceased pets and my mind went to a more ‘bad dogs get put in the pet incinerator’ situation,” one confused Redditor wrote in reply. A search of Meta’s ad database pulls up a current listing for a “Pet Animal Cremation Machine” advertised by AliExpress’s sister e-commerce site Alibaba on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Another listing , for a “Smokeless Domestic Rubbish Incinerator for Hotel Small Pet Incinerator,” was promoted by Alibaba from May until August of this year on the same platforms. Yet another listing , from late last month, advertised a “Full Combustion Pet Hospital Use Smokeless Dog & Cat Incinerator Cremator Oven.” It’s not clear whether any of those listings correspond directly to the ads seen by the users on Instagram. They don’t show the exact same product, though one of them shows a similar image of two dogs posing in front of an incineration device. candidates.title: Meta Is Using Its Massive AI Data Centers to Avoid Paying Billions of Dollars in Taxes
candidates.raw_excerpt: The AI industry’s data centers aren’t belching pollution, driving their neighbors bonkers with screeching noise, and using up vast amounts of power and water. They’re also allowing companies to exploit tax breaks to save billions of dollars on their federal tax bill. As the New York Times reports , Meta is writing off its enormous, multibillion-dollar data center construction projects as “pilot models,” a Reagan-era tax credit originally intended to support companies dabbling in potentially risky research and experimentation. Put differently, the Mark Zuckerberg-led company is telling the IRS that its data center buildouts are far from guaranteed to pay off in order to claim billions of dollars in tax credits. The news comes amid a major public backlash to the facilities, a bipartisan movement that has grown so much, it could prove influential in the upcoming midterm elections. Knowing that the companies’ plans are being used to avoid taxes is likely to infuriate an already extremely wary public. It’s also a ruse that Meta’s own accountants admit amounts to an incredibly dubious interpretation of the “pilot models” tax break. According to recent securities filings reviewed by the NYT , the company said that it may have to pay the IRS back the money it saved due to “uncertainties with our research tax credits.” There’s precedent. Thousands of companies have already been called out by the IRS for abusing the credit for regular expenses, per the newspaper’s reporting. Meta has been exploiting the loophole for two years now. In 2024, the company saved $2 billion. In its 2025 fiscal year filing, it saved almost $4 billion, making it the largest known beneficiary of the credit to date among public companies. The IRS is still trying to claw back $355 million Meta saved after exploiting another tax break loophole in 2013 for the development of its News Feed. candidates.title: China's homegrown 12,000m rig completes second ultra-deep well
candidates.raw_excerpt:
A deep well has been completed at the northern edge of China's Taklimakan Desert, marking another breakthrough in the country's ultra-deep drilling capabilities.

At 6 pm on Friday, the Zhentan-1 well, located in Wensu County, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, reached a depth of 8,345 meters. It is the second ultra-deep well drilled using China's first domestically developed 12,000-meter drilling rig.

The well is designed to explore the oil and gas potential of large structural traps in the deep northwestern Tarim Basin, particularly those dating back to the Sinian Period, and to identify new areas for expanding oil and gas reserves.

The 12,000-meter rig features an 82-meter-high steel derrick capable of handling a maximum load of 665 tonnes and is designed to drill to depths of up to 12,000 meters. Its development means China no longer needs to rely on imported rigs for drilling wells deeper than 10,000 meters.

This marks the rig's second successful application. Equipped with a 6,000-horsepower drilling drawworks, the most powerful of its kind in China, and a 900-tonne lifting system, the rig can lift a load equivalent to two high-speed train sets. Its intelligent control system enables automated operations throughout the drilling process.

candidates.title: Google launches AI-chip satellite to test performance in space
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Google launched a prototype satellite into orbit on Thursday to evaluate how its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) operate in space.

The prototype satellite, carrying four Google TPUs, was launched aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission.

Google said its team has confirmed contact with the satellite and that it is operating as expected.

Google said the launch is the first step in its Project Suncatcher, a long-term research project conducted in partnership with Planet Labs PBC to explore whether scalable machine learning infrastructure could eventually be hosted in space.

Over the coming weeks, Google will collect in-orbit data on how its TPUs handle the physical stress, radiation and thermal extremes of space. The company will use the data to refine its future designs.

In low Earth orbit, satellites can access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth, according to Google.

In the future, multiple satellite constellations could potentially be linked together, enabling them to handle larger AI workloads in orbit, the company said.

Government Officials Order the Robot Cage Fights to Stop, Organizers Say
candidates.raw_excerpt: In mid-September, a new company called Robot Entertainment Kombat hosted what it claimed was the first-ever human-on-robot cage fight in California. The whole thing was more WWE than “Real Steel” — behind the scenes, the robot was controlled by a human handler, and its strikes were sold wrastlin’-style by the dramatic human performer it “fought.” Regardless of the authenticity, the California State Athletic Commission have apparently sent the organizers a cease and desist order, addressed to “all persons holding, promoting, advertising or sponsoring unsanctioned human versus humanoid robot cage fight[s].” Using the letter to drum up some buzz on social media , Robot Entertainment Kombat founder Cix Liv seemed happy just to have the attention. “We made it boys,” he wrote. As per the letter he posted, the organizers were ordered to immediately stop hosting and promoting human-robot cage fights, or else face a misdemeanor charge. In its letter, the Athletic Commission didn’t appear to take issue with the human-robot bouts per se, but with the organizers’ failure to secure the required permits. That may be a distinction without a difference, however, as the Athletic Commission cited California business code which states that “no [full contact martial arts] event shall take place without the prior approval of the commission,” meaning the agency could simply withhold approval and veto a human-robot cage fight on a case-by-case basis — likely without ever having to explicitly declare such an event explicitly verboten. Despite the assessments still being in progress, the tech giant’s contractors started clearing trees in the area months ago, raising the alarm bells at the Finnish Nature Conservation Association. “Either this is gross incompetence from Google’s Finnish project company, Tuike Finland Oy, or gross disregard for Finnish legislation, or at worst both,” said the association’s chair, Hanna Halmeenpää, in a statement, as translated by Wood Central . Satellite images show that four separate sites were bulldozed to make way for two new data centers. Google maintains that its felling of the trees met the requirements of the country’s Forestry Act and that it had completed extensive environmental evaluations. Nonetheless, the Finnish Nature Conservation Association has since asked Finnish regulators to suspend activities until the conclusion of the ongoing environmental assessments. Halmeenpää said she was worried that local bird species may have been impacted by the area being razed. The forest also serves as a critical ecological connection, allowing animals to spread from one habitat to another. candidates.title: NorthStar Earth & Space Goes Public After SPAC Merger
candidates.raw_excerpt: Canadian space domain awareness (SDA) company NorthStar Earth & Space began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Friday morning after completing a SPAC merger this week. NorthStar completed its combination with special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Viking Acquisition Corp. I in a deal that valued NorthStar at $300 million, with an additional $30 million in private investment. NorthStar integrates ground-based and space-based data to monitor activity and detect threats in orbit. The company is headquartered in Montreal with operations in Luxembourg and New York. The company expects to use the proceeds to deploy a constellation of space-based sensors to provide SDA and space-situational awareness services to defence and commercial operators, along with ground-based sensors. “Becoming a public company gives NorthStar the resources to accelerate what we set out to build: a space-based sensor constellation that delivers trusted intelligence on the orbital environment,” said Stewart Bain, Founder and CEO of NorthStar. “We’re focused on execution as we expand the constellation and serve a growing base of government and commercial customers.” The company announced the SPAC deal in mid-April. Since then, a number of other space companies announced plans to use SPACs to go public including Quantum Space, Astrum Space, and Astro Digital just this week . candidates.title: Satlyt Secures $8M in Seed Financing
candidates.raw_excerpt: Satlyt has been boosted by securing $8 million in seed financing led by non sibi ventures . The funding will accelerate development of its virtual Al data centers in space, expand its engineering and customer delivery teams, and scale software deployments across spacecraft operated by other companies. The company announced the successful seed funding, Oct. 1. Satlyt moves more processing onto the spacecraft itself, reducing the need to send every raw image or system log to Earth for analysis. That can reduce communications demands and the wait for useful results. The company’s approach is to make computing hardware on existing spacecraft more useful through software. Operators can process data closer to where it is collected, while application developers gain a way to run their software in orbit. Over time, Satlyt aims to give spacecraft from different operators a shared software layer for coordinating computing resources. The next planned deployment is expected to support two applications on one spacecraft: research software and a commercial imagery-processing application. “Running applications on existing spacecraft gives operators a way to do more with the computing hardware they already have in orbit. Our job is to make those applications practical to deploy and operate. This financing lets us expand the engineering and delivery teams needed to support more spacecraft and customers, while building toward computing resources that can work together across missions,” Rama Afullo, founder and CEO of Satlyt, said in a statement.   The post Satlyt Secures $8M in Seed Financing appeared first on Via Satellite .

candidates.title: Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile Formally Establish Joint Venture for D2D Services
candidates.raw_excerpt: AT&T , T-Mobile , and Verizon formally established the joint venture focused on direct-to-device services the telcos first announced in May of this year. Wireless industry exec Paul Roth will serve as interim CEO during a search for a permanent CEO. The three telcos are teaming up on D2D calling for competition among satellite providers, a standards-based approach to device compatibility, and efficient use of spectrum. This comes as SpaceX has set its sights on competing with the “big three” with its next-generation Starlink Mobile service. “More satellite service providers will gain opportunities to compete, invest, and grow and the JV will work with rural mobile network operators (MNO) to enable them to bring new products to market for their customers,” Friday’s announcement said. The companies said this will result in fewer coverage gaps, improved network performance, and more access to D2D services for their customers. The JV is not exclusive, the MNOs said their existing carrier-satellite agreements will remain in place and the JV partners can continue independent connectivity efforts. The three carriers currently take different approaches to working with satellite players for D2D. T-Mobile offers service with SpaceX; AT&T is set to offer service with AST SpaceMobile; Verizon offers service on some Android phones with Skylo and has a commercial agreement with AST SpaceMobile as well. After announcing plans for the JV, the MNO CEOs made it clear they want multiple satellite options in a wholesale market for D2D. “We’ll keep pricing in check, so there isn’t a bottleneck of any particular single provider that can dictate what that pricing is,” AT&T CEO John Stankey said in May. T-Mobile CEO Srinivasan Gopalan later told investors he expects “the vast majority [of satellite] will be sourced through the JV” in the future. candidates.raw_excerpt: Eutelsat hit a milestone for its OneWeb refresh plan as Airbus Defence and Space completed the first 32 satellites in the refresh for launch. The satellites are set to be shipped for launch on a SpaceX mission; Eutelsat did not specify a timeframe. Eutelsat ordered these satellites in late 2024 as part of a 100-satellite extension . The operator has recently ordered more refresh satellites — ordering a total of 669 new OneWeb satellites for service continuity. These mark the first OneWeb satellites built in Toulouse, France. Airbus shifted manufacturing from the former joint venture Airbus OneWeb Satellites in Florida to France. The delivery is “a symbol of our industrial relocalization as well as the confirmation of our high volume, high cadence satellite delivery capability and credibility,” Alain Fauré, head of Space Systems at Airbus Defence and Space commented in a release. Eutelsat CEO Jean-François Fallacher commented that this delivery demonstrates Europe’s “ability to build and sustain a global LEO capability.” The OneWeb constellation was initially completed in 2023 , and the last OneWeb launch was an additional 20 satellites launched in October 2024 . candidates.title: Loki the sea cucumber among 57 new species found off Argentina
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Argentine scientists have identified 57 previously unknown marine species and five new genera during a deep-sea expedition in the Mar del Plata submarine canyon, the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET) said on Thursday.

The samples were collected on the "Slope 4" expedition, and it took more than a year to analyse and classify them, CONICET said.

The researchers identified 57 species that may be new to science – preliminary findings that include 20 copepods, 22 echinoderms, 14 cnidarians and one scaphopod mollusk. Five new genera of corals, sea cucumbers and crustaceans also turned up.

Among the discoveries is a deep-sea cucumber dubbed "Loki," after the Norse god, for its horn-like appendages. It's pictured above.

The "Slope 4" expedition ran for 21 days from July 23. Researchers from several Argentine universities and scientific institutions surveyed the canyon from a research vessel, using underwater exploration equipment.

candidates.title: China's first renewables mega-base in the desert goes fully online
candidates.raw_excerpt:
A power plant supporting China's first desert renewables mega base is now fully online.

Unit No.6 at the Zhongwei Power Plant in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region successfully completed a 168-hour trial run on Friday.

The milestone brings all four 660-megawatt units into operation. The plant provides support during peak electricity demand for the Ningxia Tengger Desert renewables base and the ±800-kilovolt ultra-high-voltage direct current (UHVDC) line to Hunan.

The Tengger Desert base is the first project of its kind approved by both the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration. It combines 13 million kilowatts of renewables – 4 million wind, 9 million solar – with 4.64 million kilowatts of coal-fired capacity to balance the grid.

The Zhongwei plant will provide stable back-up for the green power flowing out of the base. It smooths the gaps when wind and solar fall short by flexing its thermal output. 

The four units are designed to generate 11.8 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year and support the transmission of 22 billion kilowatt-hours of clean energy. They are expected to replace about 7.1 million tonnes of standard coal and cut carbon dioxide emissions by 18.46 million tonnes.

The plant reuses 100% of urban reclaimed water, draws no production water from the Yellow River, and keeps pollutant emissions well below national standards.

candidates.title: China develops new lithium battery material for faster charging
candidates.raw_excerpt:
A new cathode material developed by Chinese researchers could improve the fast-charging performance, durability and low-temperature operation of lithium-ion batteries.

A battery's cathode plays a key role in determining how much energy it can store, how quickly it can charge and discharge, and how long it can last. Researchers often add small amounts of specific elements to improve these properties.

A team from the Shenyang National Laboratory for Materials Science at the Institute of Metal Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences, has developed a new strategy for selecting these trace elements based on their physical and chemical properties. The findings were published Thursday in the international journal Nature Synthesis.

The researchers focused on two challenges: enabling lithium ions to move more quickly through the cathode while keeping its structure stable during repeated charging and discharging.

They found that different elements can serve different functions. Some facilitate the movement of lithium ions through the material, while others strengthen its crystal structure.

The first effect is linked to an element's ionic charge density, which affects how easily lithium ions can move through the material. Elements with lower charge density create fewer obstacles to lithium-ion movement.

The second is related to the strength of metal-oxygen bonds. Elements that form stronger bonds with oxygen can reinforce the cathode's crystal structure, helping it withstand repeated charging and discharging.

Based on these principles, the team selected magnesium, calcium, titanium and zirconium to develop a cobalt-free, high-nickel cathode containing close to 1% of each element.

candidates.title: China connects first 100-MW CO2 energy storage project to grid
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China connected its first 100-megawatt-class compressed carbon dioxide energy storage facility to the grid on Friday, marking a major breakthrough in large-capacity, zero-carbon energy storage technology.

Located in Mori Kazakh Autonomous County in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the facility can store 290 million kilowatt-hours of electricity during off-peak hours and discharge 180 million kilowatt-hours of green power during peak demand each year.

The technology functions as a massive grid-scale battery, equipped with five gas holders, 141 liquid storage units and 97 thermal storage units. It compresses carbon dioxide gas into a liquid state during periods of low electricity demand to store energy, then expands it back into gas to drive power turbines when demand peaks.

Unlike conventional pumped-hydro and compressed-air energy storage systems, the closed-loop technology does not require specific geological features such as mountains or underground caverns, offering a highly reliable, low-cost alternative for long-duration grid storage.

"Compressed carbon dioxide has a higher energy density and offers numerous advantages, including high efficiency, low cost, high safety and zero pollution," said Ma Guojiang, leader of the project.

"The project's designed efficiency makes it the most efficient carbon dioxide power generation unit in China today. candidates.raw_excerpt: First-mover advantage isn’t all it’s cracked up to be—at least, that’s the thought process for UK launch startup Skyrora. The company announced this week that it completed a 45-second hotfire test of a scaled-down version of the engine that will power the first stage of Skyrora’s orbital Skylark XL rocket. The test will inform the company’s development of the larger 70 kN engine, and Skyrora will use the data to make upgrades on the engine interface, firing operations, and tank design, according to COO Jack-James Marlow. While Skyrora is working toward a potential second flight of its suborbital Skylark L2 vehicle next year, Marlow told Payload Skyrora is “tentatively aiming for 2030 for orbital launch.” Its a big jump from last year’s projection, when Skyrora told Payload it could optimistically attempt an orbital flight as early as Q4 2026. Winning by a hare: The lengthy development path is far different from other European launch hopefuls who are racing to get past the Kármán line. But Skyrora’s pace is a feature, not a bug. “Our strategy is not to sprint towards [orbit]. We’ve seen other companies increase their opex, [and] grow drastically,” Marlow said. “I see rocket companies want to be rocket companies, rather than stable businesses. Where my view is, we’ve got to be a stable business first, rather than one, big 10-year gamble.” Skyrora was founded in 2017. Although Skyrora was quicker to get off the ground—attempting its first suborbital flight of Skylark L from Iceland in 2022—it’ll take a lot longer to get to orbit. candidates.title: Energy prices, cost of living top ASEAN energy transition concerns
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Rising energy prices and the cost of living remain the biggest concerns in Southeast Asia regarding the transition to renewable energy and the phase-down of fossil fuels, a regional survey revealed on Thursday.

About 44.6% of respondents cited surging energy prices and living costs as their biggest concerns, according to the Southeast Asia Climate Outlook Survey Report 2026, launched by Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.

This was followed by concerns over energy shortages, cited by 26.1% of respondents, the report said.

Compared with the 2024 survey, the share of respondents concerned about rising energy prices and the cost of living fell from 52.4% to 44.6% in 2026.

At the same time, concern over energy shortages rose from 20.3% in 2024 to 26.1% in 2026. The report said these concerns may reflect disruptions caused by energy shocks and geopolitical events in recent years.

The 2026 survey gathered the views of 3,706 respondents across 11 ASEAN member states. It was the first edition to include respondents from Timor-Leste, ASEAN's newest member.

candidates.title: SpaceX Dragon spacecraft carrying four astronauts docks with ISS
candidates.raw_excerpt:
SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft carrying four astronauts for NASA's Crew-13 mission docked with the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday after a nearly eight-hour journey from launch to the orbiting laboratory.

The spacecraft lifted off at 11:10 a.m. aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It autonomously docked with the ISS at 7:05 p.m.

The crew comprises NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.

The mission, codenamed Crew-13, marks the 13th crew rotation mission to the ISS conducted by a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft under NASA's Commercial Crew Program.

The crew will spend several months aboard the space station conducting scientific research and technology demonstrations to support future human exploration of the moon and Mars, as well as studies with potential benefits for people on Earth, according to NASA.

candidates.raw_excerpt:
China's commercial rocket firm CAS Space unveiled a partnership with the Guangzhou Laboratory on Monday to jointly develop space pharmaceutical payloads, with plans to conduct suborbital flight verification using a reusable spacecraft in 2027.

The first batch of payloads is slated to fly aboard the company's Lihong-2 reusable launch vehicle. The mission will conduct crystallization experiments involving proteins and small-molecule drugs, along with preliminary technical verification of space pharmaceutical hardware, the firm said.

Headquartered in Guangzhou, the laboratory focuses on research into respiratory diseases and their prevention and control. Under the partnership, the lab will define scientific research questions related to drug crystallization and oversee experimental design, sample administration, ground operations and result analysis.

Xu Qiang, a principal investigator at the laboratory, explained that modern medicine has a strong demand for higher-resolution structural data, more stable drug crystal polymorphs, human-relevant disease models and more efficient screening platforms. The space environment may open new avenues for addressing some of these challenges.

Xu pointed out that the microgravity conditions in space enable certain proteins to form higher-quality crystals and create novel experimental settings for crystal-form screening and particle regulation of small-molecule drugs. Under such conditions, cells also tend to assemble into 3D aggregates, which can be used to investigate disease mechanisms and drug responses.

candidates.raw_excerpt: NMFS is implementing annual harvest specifications and management measures for the northern subpopulation of Pacific sardine (hereafter, Pacific sardine), for the fishing year from July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027. This rule prohibits most directed commercial fishing for Pacific sardine off the coasts of Washington, Oregon, and California. Pacific sardine harvest is allowed for use only as live bait, in minor directed fisheries, as incidental catch in other fisheries, or as authorized under exempted fishing permits (EFPs). The incidental harvest of Pacific sardine will be limited to 20 percent by weight of all fish per trip when caught with other stocks managed under the Coastal Pelagic Species (CPS) Fishery Management Plan (FMP), or up to 2 metric tons (mt) per trip when caught with non-CPS stocks. The harvest specifications for 2026-2027 include an overfishing limit (OFL) of 4,645 mt, an acceptable biological catch (ABC) of 3,613 mt, an annual catch limit (ACL) of 2,200 mt, and an annual catch target (ACT) of 2,100 mt. This final rule is intended to conserve, manage, and rebuild the Pacific sardine stock off the coasts of Washington, Oregon, and California.

According to the BBC , the bizarre incident started when the 30-year-old Ye Lin sent his colleague a photo of a saltwater crocodile — entirely generated by Google Gemini — lurking in the Pandan Reservoir, a 435-acre basin in Singapore’s western residential district. To put the body of water into perspective, the Central Park Reservoir in the heart of New York City is roughly a quarter of the size, standing at just 106 acres. Though it isn’t known exactly how, Ye’s image evidently kicked off a dramatic game of telephone, which eventually made its way to officials at Singapore’s national water agency. As the BBC reports, the reservoir ended up getting shut down as water agency officials and national park staff trawled the waters in search of the nonexistent crocodile. Groups whose activities center around the reservoir, like the Singapore Canoe Federation and the Singapore Rowing Association, likewise suspended their operations as the search commenced. After examining the image with a fine-tooth comb, government officials determined it was merely a bit of AI slop, the kind which is supercharging misinformation across much of the world’s internet. Ye was then charged with “sending a false message,” a crime in Singapore bearing a maximum sentence of up to three years in prison, and a possible fine of around $8,000. StarCatcher launched Protostar, its prototype power node, which will aim to demonstrate power beaming between free-flying spacecraft. This would be the first of its kind demonstration. The mission also includes the first satellite for Meridian Space called First Customer LInk, which will test the company’s LEO communications technology. candidates.raw_excerpt: Consulting firm Analysys Mason has acquired Swedish AI and ML consultancy Modulai in a move to add specialist technical AI, ML and agentic solutions capabilities to its business. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Modulai was founded in 2018 and has a team of around 35 engineers with deep expertise in ML and agentic solutions development, including generative AI, computer vision, natural language processing, advanced recommender systems and robotics. The team develops customised ML and agentic solutions for businesses. Analysys Mason noted this acquisition will allow the company to support clients with large-scale AI transformations, AI due diligence, and AI implementation across a range of sectors. Partner Christopher Baugh noted in a LinkedIn post this will mean new capabilities and offerings for the firm’s space clients. “We have built Modulai around technical excellence and real-world AI and ML delivery. As part of Analysys Mason, we can apply that expertise at a greater scale, alongside trusted advisers to businesses, investors and governments worldwide,” Modulai co-founder and CEO Josef Lindman Hörnlund said in a statement. Analysys Mason’s business spans telecoms, digital infrastructure, space, defense, and manufacturing. The company acquired NSR, one of the leading space consulting firms, in 2022 . candidates.raw_excerpt: Iceye , the Finnish space company known for building synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites is venturing into communication satellites — planning to build sovereign satcom satellites for governments through a new partnership with Nokia . Iceye announced the move Thursday and said the first communications satellites are expected to be launched in 2028. An Iceye spokesperson said the existing Iceye satellite platform is “flexible” and now being used for satcom. Iceye has a robust business in selling SAR satellites to governments and is now expanding that offering to satcom satellites by working with Nokia. The partners plan to combine Iceye’s satellite platform and constellation experience with Nokia’s networking technology experience. The partners plan to integrate the satellites, ground infrastructure, and end-user terminals. Imagery shared by the companies shows a small, flat panel rapidly deployable terminal being used in the field, and another flat panel terminal on top of a vehicle. The aim is to provide low-latency connectivity over priority areas for governments for use cases like defense, border security, emergency services, and disaster response. Iceye stated this offering will complement existing military and commercial networks. “These are sovereign systems, so the customer determines the size of its constellation. A government acquires the satellites, ground segment, and terminals for full ownership and control, and sizes the system to its own mission needs. In the event of a scrub, a backup opportunity is available for the following day at 11:48 PM EDT. Due to the payload’s mass, Falcon Heavy’s center core, booster B1106, will be expended to maximize stage performance and ensure the classified payload is placed on the correct trajectory. B1106 will be on its first and final flight, a common practice for Falcon Heavy center cores. The outer boosters, B1072 and B1104, will land at Landing Zones 2 (LZ-2) and 1 (LZ-1), respectively. candidates.raw_excerpt: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has made the rash decision to double-down on massive AI spending, pushing a cutesy AI-mascot and poaching tech industry veteran Chirantan Desai to run a new division pushing Meta’s AI onto corporate customers. The company’s investors, however, appear to be running out of slack for Zuckerberg’s leash. Since Friday of last week, a large sell-off in Meta stocks shrunk his paper fortune by nearly $20 billion , after Goldman Sachs began raising doubts about the long-term viability of the company’s AI ambitions. Zuckerberg’s temporary losses notwithstanding — Meta’s stock is still up more than 28 percent over the last month — it does raise the question as to how much capital will be made available to satisfy the tech industry’s pie-in-the-sky AI push, and whether it can ever achieve revenue that would offset it. In addition to Goldman Sachs’ gloomy outlook for Meta, hyperscalers as a whole face what appears to be an insurmountable challenge in turning AI into a profitable venture. As Bloomberg reported , the major management consulting firm Bain and Co recently penned an analysis finding that the AI industry will need to reach an annual revenue of $6 trillion by 2031 if tech leaders continue along their current spend-happy trajectory. Doing so will require leap s in technological progress the likes of which are unprecedented in the information age — well beyond past innovations embodied by world-changing consumer tech like smartphones, for instance. If we take the cynical path and assume that the AI industry won’t be able to pull off this miracle, then any major tech firm currently doubling down — like Zuckerberg’s Meta — will have functionally spent the better part of the 2020s rigging up their own corporate noose. The robot started spinning uncontrollably, causing it to tumble back towards the Earth and burn up in the atmosphere. And now, Swift — which has been circling our planet for over two decades, providing scientists with invaluable observations of the cosmos — is about to succumb to a similar fate. The space telescope’s orbit is rapidly decaying, which will soon force NASA to wrap up the mission for good. According to an update from the agency , Swift is currently orbiting the Earth at around 200 miles. By early to mid-October, it could dip below 185 miles, a threshold below which “spacecraft operations become more difficult and science observations will likely cease.” But that hasn’t stopped scientists from eking out every bit of life out of the observatory. The team at NASA turned back on one of its three scientific instruments, the Burst Alert Telescope, which had to be shut off in April to conserve power while repositioning the spacecraft’s solar panels. They’ve also allowed the observatory to once again automatically point its telescopes at new gamma ray bursts, the extremely high-energy flashes in the sky it was primarily designed to study. candidates.title: As US relations fray, Canada gets serious about its own launch industry
candidates.raw_excerpt: A year or two ago, a few Canadian launch companies were trying to develop small rockets, but if we're being frank, the industry was not particularly notable. Sure, something interesting might eventually happen, but no one outside of a few Canadian space geeks was paying much attention. But then the Trump Administration started threatening and instituting tariffs. There was talk of making Canada the 51st state. And pretty much every Canadian I know began telling me how enraged they were at their neighbors to the south. It's hard to blame them. This has led the Canadian government to reassess all manner of areas where it had previously been happy to rely largely on the US government and American companies for goods and services. This included sovereign access to space. So this spring, the government announced the first awards to three companies—NordSpace, Reaction Dynamics, and Canada Rocket Company—to support work on rockets with "light lift" capability. candidates.title: Canada Rocket Company plans first large-scale engine test site in London, Ontario
candidates.raw_excerpt: Canada Rocket Company (CRC) will build Canada’s first large-scale rocket engine test facility at London International Airport, a $30 million complex intended for static firing of the company’s methalox engines as it develops a reusable medium-lift launch vehicle. The Jeremy Hansen Test Facility is named for Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the first Canadian to fly around the Moon. CRC will lease 50 acres from the Greater London International Airport Authority for an engine test area and a 12,000-square-foot office and shop building used for engineering, assembly, and test preparation. Putting the shop next to the stands is meant to keep engine build-up, instrumentation, and test ops in one place rather than splitting that work across distant sites. The test area is planned for up to three vertical and horizontal stands, with the ability to static-fire engines producing more than 1 MN of thrust. Vertical stands are typically used for flight-like firings. Horizontal stands are often used earlier in a campaign for access, instrumentation, and engine development work. CRC said the site is a foundational step toward sovereign Canadian launch capability. The company expects the facility to be fully operational by 2028 and said it is working with the airport, regulators, and the local community as planning advances. CRC is developing a reusable medium-lift rocket capable of delivering up to 12,500 kg to sun-synchronous orbit, powered by its own E-1 methalox engine. candidates.title: Mate 90: Faster chips without the tools Huawei can't buy
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Huawei can't buy the machines that make the world's most advanced chips. So it redesigned the chip.

The Kirin 9050 Pro, launched inside the Mate 90 series on Thursday, is one of the first commercial processors built on LogicFolding – an architecture Huawei unveiled in May as the practical core of its "Tau Scaling Law." The company positions it as a successor to Moore's Law, as transistor shrinks approach physical and economic limits.

Instead of shrinking transistors, LogicFolding stacks two active circuit layers and links them with millions of vertical interconnects, shortening the distance signals must travel between logic blocks.

That answers a constraint Huawei consumer chief Richard Yu acknowledged days before the launch: "Advanced semiconductor capacity remains very limited in China," where chipmakers still depend on deep ultraviolet lithography rather than the extreme ultraviolet tools used at the leading edge.

Yu framed it in a single line: "Moore's Law pursues smaller transistors; Tau's Law pursues shorter, faster signal paths." CGTN previously described the approach as a move "from geometry to time," optimizing signal delay instead of transistor density.

The results are substantial. The Kirin 9050 Pro carries 5 million signal bonding points and delivers 125 TB/s of inter-die bandwidth. Huawei claims a 31% performance gain over the previous flagship generation, with critical-path latency cut by more than 30% – a figure that matters more for sustained workloads than peak benchmarks.

candidates.title: Juice’s September 2026 Earth flyby: the movie
candidates.raw_excerpt: Video: 00:00:48 On 28 September 2026, ESA’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer ( Juice ) successfully completed a gravity assist flyby of Earth. Flight controllers guided the spacecraft close to our home planet to increase its velocity by 3.5 km/s and deflect its trajectory by an angle of 20°. As Juice flew just 8640 km above the Indian Ocean, it snapped a series of images with its onboard monitoring cameras, giving us a unique ‘Juice eye view’ of our home planet. Juice’s monitoring cameras provide 1024 x 1024 pixel snapshots that can be processed in colour. Their main purpose is to monitor the spacecraft’s various booms and antennas, especially during the challenging period after launch. The photos they captured of Earth during the flyby are a bonus. In the first seconds of the video we see a view from Juice monitoring camera 2 – or JMC2 – with Earth appearing as a thin crescent at the bottom right of the frame. Around 10 seconds in, we switch to a view from JMC1, with almost the entire disc of Earth visible at the top right of the frame. The large land mass that we see is Africa. Even the Moon is visible as a tiny grey dot to Earth’s right. At the very end of the video, JMC1 gives us a final view of Earth in the distance as it flies away on 29 September. candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s practically impossible these days to attend a concert without a flood of bright smartphone screens obscuring your view. In a desperate bid to shore up street cred with their followers on social media, audience members simply cannot help themselves from documenting every little thing, going as far as to record videos of entire songs — a practice that comes directly at the cost of their fellow concertgoers’ sanity. This screen-filled nightmare has now caught the attention of Grammy-winning singer songwriter Phoebe Bridgers. For her latest tour, she implemented a strict phone ban — including smartwatches and Meta’s “ pervert glasses ” — to put the music front and center. The result, so far, has been a far more memorable couple of hours that are inspiring a smartphone-obsessed generation to get creative in ways that have already been unexpectedly beautiful. Some fan have pulled out pencils and pens to physically sketch Bridgers’ stage and lighting, a wholesome example of what we stand to gain by setting aside our ever-present depression rectangles. “Went by myself so figured I’d draw while I was there!” one fan wrote in a Reddit post , alongside other amateur artists doing their best . “Such a great concert, the lighting effects were so cool and also the way they used the dome thing on the main stage throughout.” “Having no phones made all the lighting effects pop way more and people got their lighters out to wave them back and forth for the sad songs like in the olden days!” the user added. It’s not just Bridgers. A growing contingent of artists are forcing audience members to lock up their valuables in Yondr pouches, which are secure, lockable fabric bags intended for smartphone-free spaces that have cropped up in event halls, schools , and even court rooms . candidates.title: Norwegian Government Proposes Paying for Second Andøya Launch Pad
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: Isar Aerospace The Norwegian government plans to invest almost NOK 650 million (almost €60 million) to build a second orbital launch pad at Andøya Spaceport. The state will own the pad and lease it to Andøya Space, the commercial operator of the orbital launch facility. Norway’s Minister of Trade and Industry, Cecilie Myrseth, announced the planned investment during a 30 September event hosted by Norway’s Directorate for Space Activities. Christian Hauglie-Hanssen, Director General of the Norwegian Space Agency, later said the government would allocate an initial NOK 323.3 million for the new pad in its 2027 budget proposal. The remainder of the planned amount will then be included in the government’s 2028 budget. According to Norway’s national news agency NTB , responsibility for building the new pad will be given to Forsvarsbygg, the Norwegian Defence Estates Agency. Once built, the pad will be leased to Andøya Space, a commercial entity in which the state holds a 90% stake. Additionally, the Norwegian Armed Forces will be tasked with securing the area around the spaceport, similar to the role played by the French military at the Guiana Space Centre. The plan outlined by Minster Myrseth appears to mark a shift from the government’s initial approach to building out a second launch pad. In a proposal published earlier this year, the government said Andøya Spaceport’s business model envisaged two launch pads, with construction of the second dependent on Andøya Space securing a long-term contract with another launch provider. Under the new arrangement, the Norwegian state will instead bear the cost and retain ownership of the infrastructure. More details on how the project will be financed, including where the funding will be drawn from, are expected when the government publishes its 2027 state budget on 7 October. candidates.title: Top BBC Director Says He’s Been Reviewing a Fully AI-Generated Episode of “Doctor Who” and It’s “Pretty Good”
candidates.raw_excerpt: Slipping ratings, a revolving door of lead actors, and nothing quite hitting like that old school David Tennant run. It’s dog days for “Doctor Who” fans, whose lives aren’t likely to be made any better by the prospect of AI creeping into the show. While speaking at the Royal Television Society conference in London, BBC director Matt Brittin extolled the amazing efficiency of using AI to crank out footage — before raising the possibility of using it on one of the British broadcaster’s most beloved series. “Everyone’s got the ability in their hands — or six billion people have — to create content at the standard of a Hollywood studio,” Brittin said, as quoted by Variety . “Somebody sent me a 50-minute episode of ‘Doctor Who’ that was AI-generated the other day. It’s pretty good,” he continued. “I mean, it’s not going to replace humans, and we’ll come on to that. So everyone’s a creator.” Brittin, it’s worth noting, was president of Europe, Middle East, and Africa operations at Google — a major purveyor of AI tech — before joining the BBC . You have to wonder what Brittin’s idea of “pretty good” is. Attempts at using AI to crank out a movie or short film have invariably produced low grade slop . While the tech can sometimes create realistic images or scenes in isolation, cobbling together disparate, screensaver-worthy images together doesn’t constitute an episode of hit television. There’s a reason that filmmakers and other artists have turned their noses up at AI , along with the small matter of the tech threatening to drive them out of their jobs, and the fact that it was trained on their artwork and performances without permission. The ones that do use it get are often lampooned as hacks, has-beens or sellouts . And for “Doctor Who,” a show that’s sputtering along on its 41st season and is currently on hiatus as it searches for new ideas, the last thing it needs at this creatively critical impasse is the injection of a tool that recycles old ideas without direction

candidates.title: China's Shenzhou-23 astronauts send National Day greetings from space
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The Shenzhou-23 astronauts aboard China's space station sent video greetings to their motherland on Thursday, which marks China's National Day and the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.

Commander Zhu Yangzhu and his crewmates Zhang Zhiyuan and Li Jiaying, or Lai Ka-ying in Cantonese, delivered their wishes for the country and its space program together as the space station, about 400 km above Earth, flew over China.

"When we look at Earth from the space station, that brilliantly lit land is the motherland we miss day and night," said Li, the first astronaut from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region to travel to space.

The three astronauts were launched aboard the Shenzhou-23 spaceship late on May 24 and have been in orbit for more than four months. They are in good condition, having completed in-orbit crew rotation with the Shenzhou-21 astronauts, repaired the station's solar panels in a spacewalk and deployed application payloads outside the station.

This year marks the 70th anniversary of the founding of China's space program. Remarkable milestones include the launch of the country's first satellite, Dongfanghong-1, the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System that offers global services, the Chang'e lunar missions, the Tianwen-1 Mars mission, the space station and the steady advance of crewed lunar exploration project.

"We can never forget that in deserts, mountains and on islands, a group of people have gazed at the stars and kept striving, generation after generation, for 70 years, creating the glory of China's space program," said Zhang, who is on his first spaceflight.

candidates.title: Satlyt Raises $8M Seed to Expand Its Virtual ODC Network
candidates.raw_excerpt: While investors pour billions of dollars into orbital-data-center (ODC) concepts that require new feats of engineering, Satlyt’s virtual ODC network is already flying above us—and growing rapidly. The startup—with joint headquarters in Nairobi, Kenya, and Sunnyvale, CA—unveiled a $8M seed round today to expand its team and its virtual ODC network. non sibi ventures led the round, which included additional participation from TLCOM, Antler, Slauson & Co., Launch Africa Ventures, Enza Capital, Demos Capital, BAG Collective, Gaingels, Askya, AXIAN Investment and others. It brings Satlyt’s total funds to “well past $10M,” according to CEO Rama Afullo. Meet Satlyt: Satlyt was founded in 2024 by Afullo, an alum of SpaceX and Google who spent years trying to convince both companies to invest in in-space edge computing opportunities. “I was pitching orbital data centers at Google three years ago…I was pitching it at SpaceX [Starlink] right after that…And in both cases, I was getting turned down,” Afullo told Payload. The pitch was simple. As satellites fly overhead, they gather far too much data to downlink efficiently and affordably. Satlyt’s solution is to inject AI-inference capabilities on board partner satellites—either by pre-programming them before launch, or uploading the software in-flight—to process data in orbit, and downlink only the most necessary data outputs. In November, Satlyt won a NASA STTR contract with a total value of $4M to design delay-tolerant edge protocols in space. In May the company announced it had notched its biggest in-space success. Satlyt demonstrated its ability to run AI inference software in space—using Google’s Gemma AI model—and validated that Satlyt’s system “processed imagery, generated an encrypted downlink-ready output, and diagnosed multiple injected software faults,” Afullo said in a post on LinkedIn. candidates.title: Starfish Otter, other payloads set to launch on Transporter 18
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX plans to launch a Transporter rideshare mission aboard a Falcon 9 from California, on the same day as the Crew-13 and NROL-97 Falcon Heavy missions out of Florida. This will be the first time in a while that the company is using all three Falcon-capable launch pads in the same general time period. Transporter 18 is scheduled to fly on Thursday, Oct. 1 at 11:18 AM PDT (18:18 UTC) from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base. The 58-minute launch window ends at 12:16 PM PDT (19:16 UTC), and if the schedule holds, this will be the 110th Falcon 9 mission of 2026. The mission’s 130 payloads feature a prototype AI satellite for Google, the NASA-funded SPRITE telescope, and Starfish’s first Otter servicing vehicle, among others. The rocket will take a southerly trajectory suitable for sun-synchronous orbiting payloads. Following stage separation, the first stage, B1082-25, will conduct a return-to-launch-site maneuver before touching down at Landing Zone 4 near its launch pad. The booster started its career with the Starlink 7-9 mission and launched on 20 additional Starlink flights, as well as the USSF-62, OneWeb #20, and NROL-145 missions. Artist’s impression of the SPRITE satellite in orbit. (Credit: University of Colorado/LASP) After the second stage finishes the second burn of its Merlin Vac engine at T+51:07, the mission’s payloads will be released during an 11-minute period from T+54:22 to T+1:05:15. NASA’s SPRITE payload will start off the deployment sequence, and the separation of Varda Space’s W-8 space factory will mark the final release. Google’s Project Suncatcher M1 prototype, set to deploy at T+1:01:25, is an experimental satellite to test data processing hardware in orbit for future space-based AI data centers. The satellite will evaluate how Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) handle launch vibrations and space radiation, as well as approaches to cooling the chips. candidates.title: Foundational Raises £8.2M for Satellite Laser Ranging
candidates.raw_excerpt: Foundational wants to turn bouncing lasers off satellites into a commercial service.  The London startup emerged from stealth today with an £8.2M ($10.8M) pre-seed round—which it says is Europe’s largest space-tech pre-seed to date.  Investors include early-stage VC firms Inflection, BACKED, and Adjacent, alongside Type One Ventures and Final Frontier, a European fund focused on defense, space, and cyber. Origin story: Foundational CEO Hira Virdee founded SSA data company Lumi Space in 2018, which was focused on pure R&D and government projects. Last year, he partnered with CTO Dave Gooding to cofound Foundational to commercialize the tech, bringing Lumi in as a subsidiary. “From the company formation to landing the term sheet and closing the investment was very, very quick,” Virdee told Payload. “I think a lot of that was testament to the previous work.”  Mirror, mirror: Foundational is automating and scaling satellite laser ranging (SLR), a highly precise method for measuring the distance to satellites. The company likens its accuracy to detecting a car in Edinburgh rolling forward by the width of a pencil—from a viewpoint in London. Its system combines three pieces:   Retroreflectors on satellites, which keep working even after a satellite dies; Automated ground stations that fire laser pulses at them and time the light’s return; A software platform that processes and delivers the data. SLR dates back to the 1960s, but legacy stations are expensive and require staff. candidates.title: Space Insurer Charter Space Raises $5M Seed Round
candidates.raw_excerpt: You can bundle your home and auto insurance with the click of a button, but covering your spacecraft has traditionally been a little trickier. CA-based Charter Space is working to increase access to insurance products for companies developing new missions in space, and yesterday it announced a $5M seed round to accelerate its market traction. Crystal Venture Partners led the round, which included participation from QED, Blank Ventures, Gaingels, Hustle Fund and others. The round brings Charter’s total financing to $8M since its founding in 2021.   In good hands: Before Charter came along, insuring spacecraft was a long and expensive undertaking, as underwriters—often without technical backgrounds—had to manually evaluate the combined risk of hundreds of subcomponents. The process kept space insurance largely out-of-reach to all but the most expensive missions—Charter CEO Yuk Chi Chan estimated earlier this year that ~97% of spacecraft in orbit are flying around uninsured. The Charter Interplanetary Risk Corporation (CIRC)—Charter’s own insurance brokerage for space companies—has been able to shorten this underwriting process by leaning on the technical expertise it gained through its space program management tool—called Ubik—which engineers rely on to build next-gen missions. CIRC married the data from Ubik with an AI-powered underwriting tool to shorten the time it takes to secure a policy, from months to approximately two weeks. And now, the company can hardly keep up with the wave of demand. Ultimately, Charter hopes that by making insurance more accessible to small- and medium-sized spacecraft, the market will respond by flying more missions and reaching further away from Earth.  “Strong insurance options give American space companies the confidence to invest, grow, and take on new challenges. candidates.title: Data Centers Are a $6 Trillion Time Bomb, Analysts Warn
candidates.raw_excerpt: Last year, hedge fund whisperer and founder of the firm Praetorian Capital, Harris Kupperman, issued a blistering financial analysis on the data center frenzy sweeping across the United States. Kupperman’s diagnosis was blunt: because data center components break down so quickly, the industry would need to see some $1 trillion in revenue across 2025 and 2026 just to cover the costs of their hyperscale facilities, let alone start turning a profit. With AI revenue today accounting for only a small fraction of that total, Kupperman’s argument is that the financial logic behind the data center buildout simply doesn’t hold up. But as the last year has shown us, the magnates of the AI industry — and their funders — have a remarkable knack for kicking the can down the road, no matter how bad the numbers might look . That being the case, analysts are starting to use Kupperman’s same rationale to forecast what the next few years have in store for data center developers — and the numbers are staggering. As Bloomberg reports , an analysis on data centers by Bain and Co, one of the largest management consulting firms in the world, found that the global AI industry would have to reach annual revenue of $6 trillion by 2031 to justify the amount of capital being injected into data centers. The analysis assumes that commercial AI tools will account for $1.8 trillion of revenue by that point — a pretty generous presumption, which requires global AI revenue to start growing almost exponentially. Even if the AI industry reaches that point, Bain’s analysis notes, the industry will still need to come up with $4.2 trillion. Hitting that $6 trillion mark will take nothing short of a technological miracle, the report authors explain, a leap without precedent in the information age. “What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” the report’s lead author and chairman of Bain’s Global Technology, Media, and Telecommunications, David Craw

candidates.raw_excerpt: An attempt to save NASA's $500 million Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory from dropping out of orbit fell short, but the behind-the-scenes machinations required just to make a rescue possible deserve recognition, government and commercial space officials said in a recounting of the mission. The rescue mission was developed by Katalyst Space Technologies, working under a $30 million contract awarded by NASA last September. NASA gave Katalyst nine months to build and launch a satellite to capture Swift flying some 200 miles above the Earth and boost it into a higher orbit. Katalyst's rescue spacecraft, known as Link, successfully launched July 3 and completed some of its initial checkouts before a malfunction caused it to spin out of control a few weeks later. candidates.title: Crew-13 astronauts launch to ISS after weeks of delays
candidates.raw_excerpt: One veteran astronaut and three first-time flyers began a six-month mission to the International Space Station as part of the NASA and SpaceX Crew-13 mission. NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, as well as Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, launched on Thursday, Oct. 1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. This mission also marked the shortest time between launch and docking for any Crew Dragon vehicle. Crew Dragon C213, named Grace , flew on its second-ever mission and its first long-duration stay at the orbiting laboratory. It first flew in June 2025 as part of the Axiom-4 mission and spent just over 20 days in space. With the on-time launch at 11:10 AM EDT (15:10 UTC) on Oct. 1, the crew spent less than eight hours free-flying before their capsule autonomously docked with the forward port of the Station’s Harmony module. The previous record was set by Crew-11, which made the journey in just under 15 hours. Issues with the capsule pushed the launch from a Sept. 12 attempt to its current date. According to NASA, during standard prelaunch spacecraft processing, an oxidizer leak was found in Dragon’s propulsion system. The Crew Dragon vehicle is equipped with 16 Draco thrusters for on-orbit maneuvering. It utilizes hypergolic propellants, meaning they ignite upon contact with each other. SpaceX uses monomethyl hydrazine as fuel and nitrogen tetroxide as oxidizer. They also participated in a dry dress rehearsal on Sept. 29, which involved running through all the launch-day activities up to liftoff with no propellants loaded into the rocket. candidates.title: Miller Tapped to Head SPACECOM, Oversee Move To Huntsville
candidates.raw_excerpt: The White House on Tuesday nominated U.S. Space Force Lt. Gen. David Miller for his fourth star as the head of U.S. Space Command (SPACECOM). Miller would replace Gen. Stephen Whiting as SPACECOM commander. Since last November, Miller has served as the deputy chief of space operations for strategy, plans, programs and requirements. Before that, Miller was the final head of Space Operations Command (SpOC). Last November, Space Force changed SpOC’s name to Combat Forces Command (CFC) to signal a move “toward enhanced combat readiness and integrated space defense.” CFC’s legacy dates back to Air Force Space Command, which became SpOC in October 2020. In September last year, Miller spoke of the first space electromagnetic warfare tactical operations center and coming advances in space control, orbital warfare , and the surveillance, tracking, and targeting of potential adversary air and space systems — a foreshadowing of Air Force Secretary Troy Meink’s statement on the existence of U.S. orbital weapons at the Air & Space Forces Association’s conference this month. If confirmed by the Senate as head of SPACECOM, Miller will have oversight of the command’s move from Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado, to Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama — a move that was the subject of a bitter partisan battle on Capitol Hill. candidates.title: Trusted Computing Group Creates Key New Working Group Focusing on Aerospace Security
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Trusted Computing Group (TCG) has created a new Aerospace and Non-Terrestrial Systems Solutions Working Group (AERO-SWG) as it looks to play a key role in keeping satellite systems secure. Focusing on satellite networks, unmanned systems, autonomous platforms, and disconnected edge environments, AERO-SWG will aim to help operators apply trusted computing principles to strengthen the resilience and integrity of the systems now central to global communications and critical infrastructure. TCG announced the new group, Sept. 29. AERO-SWG will aim to establish trust within the devices, platforms, gateways, and supply chains that underpin the global communications, defense, transportation, and critical infrastructure society now relies upon. This will be achieved through practical guidance, gap analysis, and recommendations to existing TCG Work Groups. The group will be chaired by TCG member Thorsten Stremlau of Nvidia. AERO-SWG will explore how layered hardware and firmware security can be applied across aircraft, satellites and ground stations to strengthen trust at the platform level. This includes Trusted Platform Modile (TPM)-based Roots-of-Trust for flight-critical software, Device Identifier Composition Engine (DICE) for lightweight subsystem protection, and CyRes for restoring corrupted firmware in flight or in orbit. “AERO-SWG gives the industry a dedicated forum to ensure trusted computing in the toughest aerospace environments, including satellites and autonomous systems. By bringing experts together to focus on practical needs and real deployment barriers, the group will help accelerate the development of secure and interoperable technologies in this crucial sector,” Joe Pennisi, president of TCG, said in a statement. The post Trusted Computing Group Creates Key New Working Group Focusing on Aerospace Security appeared first on Via Satellite .

candidates.title: RFK Jr Announcing That AI Is Now Better Than Human Doctors Shows That He Is a Buffoon Who Is Ruining Trust in American Health Institutions
candidates.raw_excerpt: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. doesn’t trust human doctors, but he does trust AI chatbots — and so should you, he’s using his authority as chief medical spokesperson in the US government to tell the public. The crux of the health secretary’s recent remarks during his “fireside chat” with vice president JD Vance at the Make America Healthy Again Conference on Tuesday was that AI models are now “better informed” than physicians, empowering ordinary Americans to second guess what their doctor tells them at every turn. AI, he proclaimed, has the power “to free us from medical tyranny,” the New York Times reported . It’s not an unsurprising line from a man whose distrust of scientific medicine stems from the fact that it disagrees with his crank health beliefs , which range from vaccine “skepticism” to promoting a red meat heavy diet. What’s more illuminating is how the Kennedy scion is explicitly touting AI as a way of undermining the medical establishment. “One of the things that is going to change is that we’re never ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us, ‘Trust the experts,'” Kennedy said, as quoted by the NYT . “If somebody tells you, ‘Masks work, trust the experts,’ AI may tell you otherwise,” he continued. “If somebody tells you, ‘Social distancing works, trust the experts,’ AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, or you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say it actually doesn’t do that.” At one point, Kennedy claimed that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had personally told him that it would be “malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or make a prescription without at least checking AI.” Many doctors, it’s true, do use AI tools for taking clinical notes, transcribing patient visits, and even looking up symptoms. One widely used medical AI tool called OpenEvidence is already used by around two thirds of physicians in the US, according to its internal data.

candidates.title: New Jersey So Flooded That a Shark Was Spotted Swimming Through a Suburban Neighborhood
candidates.raw_excerpt: A shark has been spotted wandering the streets of New Jersey. And it ain’t here for the vig , either. With the powerful nor’easter storm battering the Eastern Seaboard over the weekend, floodwaters have poured into the perhaps unfortunately named town of Surf City, turning its suburban streets into aquatic thoroughfares. Marine traffic obliged. In a viral video taken Saturday by a local resident, a shark — as in the fish, not the mobsters who enforce usurious loans— is seen swimming through the town like it owns the place. The shark’s dorsal fin, in cinematic fashion, even breaks through the surface of the water. “Is that a little shark?” one person can be heard saying, almost in disbelief. “It’s coming this way!” Fortunately, this is almost certainly no man-eater. According to Greg Skomal, a white shark researcher with the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries, the shark in the video appears to be a smooth dogfish — “which is a very small, harmless shark that is common in those waters,” he told ABC News . After patrolling the resident’s driveway, the shark reportedly started swimming toward Barnegat Bay, according to ABC , seemingly content with making its presence known. A snowless nor’easter over the weekend has ravaged parts of the east coast, with New Jersey and New York among the hardest hit states, where both governors have declared states of emergency for specific locales.  Strong winds exceeding 60 miles per hour knocked trees over, killing a 56-year-old man in Brooklyn. Flooding was reported all over New Jersey, seeping into resident’s homes. On the more lighthearted side of things, many an opportunistic kayaker has pounced on the chance to traverse their towns on narrow boats. An entire 19th century shipwreck was even unearthed by the storm. And now sharks, apparently, are enjoying the sightseeing occasion of a lifetime.
