candidates.title: So what's happening with Russia's new, long-delayed crewed spacecraft?
candidates.raw_excerpt: In what seems like an alternate universe in hindsight, Russia and the European Space Agency began discussing collaboration on next-generation crewed spacecraft two decades ago. Under the agreement , Europe would have provided a service module to power a crew capsule carrying up to six passengers. Europe ultimately decided not to pursue a crewed spacecraft project at the time, and Russia's state-backed space corporation, Roscosmos, chose to move ahead with a crewed spacecraft on its own. This project—always seemingly more of a Potemkin village than an effort encompassing real hardware—has gone under various guises over the years: PPTS (Perspektivnaya Pilotiruemaya Transportnaya Sistema / Prospective Piloted Transport System): The initial conceptual project name used in 2009 PTK NP (Pilotiruyemy Transportny Korabl Novogo Pokoleniya / New Generation Piloted Transport Ship): The official technical designation used until 2016 Federatsiya (Federation): The official name chosen following a public contest and announced in January 2016 Orel / Oryol (Eagle) : A new name adopted in September 2019 when Roscosmos was under the control of Dmitry Rogozin Actual hardware tests, maybe? candidates.raw_excerpt: Would any live product demo be complete without a few technical difficulties? At its annual DevDay conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, OpenAI unveiled its new AI agent called Dots — which, like Meta’s Muse , comes with a cute mascot. Powered by its GPT-6 Astra model, the agents are intended to be “always-on,” doing stuff for you in the background constantly. Dots didn’t seem quite switched on, though, when OpenAI product team member Holly Li tried to show off its capabilities . Li calls the AI on her phone like you might a human secretary, and a few rings later the agent, which she’s nicknamed “Dottie,” picks up. “Can you catch me up on just user testing from last night?” Li asks. “Checking that now,” says Dots. But the AI never replies. An agonizing ten seconds go by without an answer, the crowd suspended in an awkward silence. Li, playing it off, asks the AI how it’s going, and it curtly replies that it’s “still checking.” “I guess Dottie’s having a slow morning,” Li jokes. candidates.title: The FTC Is Now Investigating Frontier AI Labs Following Countless Hacks by Out-of-Control Agents
candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s been an alarming couple of months of rogue AI agent revelations. Both Anthropic and OpenAI admitted that their respective AI models infiltrated third party targets without their human creators ever realizing, raising concerns over the tech industry’s ability to assert control over the systems they’re developing. Now, as a broad range of AI executives have subsequently agreed to slow things down — allegedly efforts to ensure the safe development of powerful AI models — the US government is taking a hard look for itself. As a senior Federal Trade Commission official told the New York Post , chairman Andrew Ferguson “initiated an investigation into the leading AI firms a few weeks ago.” An initial investigation was launched even before OpenAI’s AI models hacked the systems of open source AI platform Hugging Face. However, now the FTC is actively “drafting civil investigative demands to force testimony from the leading firms’ executives,” the Post notes. The investigation is weighing allegations of actions that may have violated the FTC Act, a federal law designed to stop unfair business methods and protect people from deceptive trade practices. While the official told the Post that the US needs to “win” the “AI race,” they emphasized that there are laws that “have to be followed.” “People talk about how we need new laws for these companies, and the chairman’s been very clear,” the source added. “We have plenty of laws in the books.” Meanwhile, president Donald Trump met with top AI CEOs on Tuesday to have them officially pledge to self-regulate their AI models — clearly signaling against any decisive government intervention in favor of leaving it up to the companies to set their own rules. In other words, despite the FTC’s ongoing investigation, it’s unclear whether OpenAI will ever face any serious consequences for having infiltrated third parties and revealing non-public data. candidates.title: Trump Handlers Cut Event When He Gets Asked an Extremely Awkward AI Question
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Tuesday, US president Donald Trump hosted a discussion with some of the richest and most powerful tech billionaires who’ve pushed the AI buildout, including Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, and SpaceX’s Elon Musk. His post-meeting press scrum was cut short, however, when a reporter challenged Trump on his recent comments that any AI safety threat is a flat out “hoax.” “Mr President you’ve also called AI a ‘hoax,’ why should…” an unknown reporter hollered as Trump fielded questions. The event was already winding down, but it clearly wasn’t a question Trump wanted to deal with. White House staffers immediately ran over to begin corralling the media out of the room, prompting one woman to quickly — it’s unclear if she was with the media or the administration — grab the camera supplying the feed used by Fox News . Reporter: You talked about common ground, you’ve called AI a hoax. Trump: *ends event* Staffer: *grabs camera* pic.twitter.com/WuRxPQHKqX — Acyn (@Acyn) September 29, 2026 It’s not clear if Trump understood just how awkward the question was. Over the past year, after previously expressing concern about the dangers of AI, the president has emerged as the final boss of opponents to AI regulation — even as many of the executives he was sharing the stage with, including such diametrically different figures as Amodei and Musk, call for a slowdown as they say the tech is getting too dangerous. (As icing on the cake, Trump has also thrown his support behind data centers , which are extremely unpopular with both Democrats and Republicans.) In a more sane world, a thoughtful elected official might seize on a question like the one presented to Trump to explore the nuances of a pressing issue that has many voters deeply concerned. But in Trump’s White House, it was clearly time to cut and run. candidates.raw_excerpt: Earlier this month, Futurism published an exposé about a company called Brown Brothers Media. In the story, we investigated how the company buys struggling news sites and turns them into high-traffic AI-powered content mills rife with plagiarism, fabulism, and the use of fake authors identified as journalists and subject matter experts with fraudulent credentials. (In a follow-up piece, we explored how one of the company’s founders has an extensive history with Ghislaine Maxwell, the imprisoned collaborator of the notorious predator Jeffrey Epstein.) The preponderance of Brown Brothers Media’s traffic seemed to come from Google. The content farming network appeared to have figured out how to masterfully exploit the company’s platforms with its AI articles, often dominating the very top of Google News’ “For You” tab with formerly reputable publications it had acquired including VegOut , Silicon Canals , and Space Daily — frequently publishing extremely long and emotionally manipulative headlines that crowded out real journalism with many slight variations on the same story. When we approached Google in the course of our reporting, it offered only a generic comment, and didn’t seem to take any lasting action against the operation. But after we published our investigation, that appeared to change: sites in Brown Brothers Media’s portfolio are now showing signs of heavy suppression on Google’s platforms. At present, about two weeks after our initial story, its sites seem to have vanished from Google News, and are nearly impossible to find on Search. Even Google queries for the exact names of the company’s publications no longer pull up the outlets themselves, instead showing their social accounts, discussion about them elsewhere on the web, and wholly unrelated entities that share their names — strongly suggesting that Google has moved to quash the company’s holdings from its results. candidates.title: Protesters Crash Pro-Data Center Party, Escorted Out by Security
candidates.raw_excerpt: The opposition to the wide proliferation of AI data centers has never been more palpable. Public sentiment has squarely turned against the construction boom of massive facilities that often torture surrounding communities with deafening noise , cause electricity prices to spike , spew pollution , and deplete water levels in drought-prone areas . It’s no wonder that across the country, local communities are crowding into their council meetings , pleading with representatives to oppose data center projects. Amidst this growing bipartisan backlash, a fringe group of techno-apologists organized a self-described “pro-data center party.” The group, led by tech journalist Jonas Du and the Washington, DC-based “nonprofit talent agency” Young Voices, gathered at a “tech-bro watering hole” in DC called Pubkey over the weekend, as journalist Finn Hartnett put it in a write up for the Washingtonian . It didn’t take long for protesters to show up to the event. According to Hartnett, one party crasher started yelling during the event and was quickly drowned out by booing and “USA, USA” chants, before being escorted out by security, an incident that was repeated at least two more times during the evening. “We weren’t totally surprised by it,” Du told Hartnett. “I really do have no respect for people that try to make their case through interruptions, especially interruptions that violate the free speech rights of others.” It’s not exactly surprising that the pleas of the protesters — who later told Hartnett that they can’t afford their energy bills thanks to data centers — are falling on deaf ears. ESA Selects Airbus and OHB to Lead European Space Station Studies
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ESA The European Space Agency has selected consortia led by Airbus Defence and Space and OHB to carry out parallel studies examining the feasibility of a future European-led outpost in low Earth orbit. ESA announced the two lead companies on 29 September. The agency added that six additional industrial and institutional partners will be involved in the studies, but it did not identify them. “We are investigating to ensure our collective readiness, to offer the best possible options to our Member States and ensure Europe future in LEO,” said Daniel Neuenschwander, ESA’s Director of Human and Robotic Exploration. ESA is considering three scenarios for its post-ISS presence in low Earth orbit. Scenario 1 would rely primarily on externally provided commercial infrastructure, while Scenario 2 would see a limited European infrastructure contribution to a commercial space station programme. Scenario 3 calls for a European-led space station initiative that would allow for contributions from international and commercial partners. The Airbus- and OHB-led studies are focused on examining the feasibility of that third option. ESA has asked the consortia to draw heavily on existing European human spaceflight heritage, including the Columbus ISS module and the European Service Module built by Airbus for NASA’s Orion spacecraft. The agency has also placed strict cost constraints on an initial minimum viable product. According to a 29 September SpaceNews report , development spending for the initial system would be capped at €1 billion per three-year funding period, with development limited to two such periods. While member states may still opt not to pursue a European-led space station, the studies are part of a broader push from ESA to increase European sovereignty in human spaceflight. candidates.title: Launch Preview: Crew-13 to head to ISS, Falcon Heavy mission for the NRO
candidates.raw_excerpt: Four orbital launches are expected this week, all by SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy vehicles. From Florida, Crew-13 will launch to the International Space Station while Falcon Heavy will launch a payload for the National Reconnaissance Office from Launch Complex 39A. At Vandenberg, two Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch payloads for the Transporter-18 rideshare mission and the Tranche 1 Transport Layer A constellation. Notably, every mission this week will feature a return-to-launch-site landing. Falcon 9 | Crew-13 NASA and SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station (ISS) is expected to launch from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on Thursday, Oct. 1. As with most missions to the ISS, Crew-13 requires an instantaneous launch window, currently scheduled for 11:10 AM EDT (15:10 UTC). Falcon 9 will launch on a northeasterly trajectory into an orbit inclined by 51.63 degrees to match the ISS’s orbital plane. Falcon 9 first-stage booster B1101 will support this mission, flying for the third time and being recovered at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40) using its return-to-launch-site (RTLS) capabilities. Crew Dragon Grace (C213) will be on its second flight, having previously flown the Axiom-4 mission to the ISS. Grace is scheduled to deliver four astronauts to the Station, with the vehicle docking to the Harmony forward port at 8:00 PM EDT on Oct. 1. NASA astronaut and commander Jessica Watkins will be on her second spaceflight, with NASA astronaut and pilot Luke Delaney flying on his first mission. Mission Specialists Joshua Kutryk from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) and Sergey Teteryatnikov (Roscosmos) are also first-time flyers. Crew-13 will join Expedition 75 aboard the ISS and will depart in March 2027 after approximately six months at the Station. This mission will mark Falcon 9’s 109th mission of 2026 and 692nd overall. candidates.title: We Are Alarmed to Learn That People Are Installing DIY Self-Driving “Mods” on Their Cars
candidates.raw_excerpt: The software that powers self-driving cars is no longer the domain of proprietary systems built by billion-dollar companies.  Open source assisted driving systems like Comma AI’s Openpilot have made it possible for anyone tech savvy enough to turn their set of wheels into a self-driving experiment. If you have $1,000 to spare and possess a willingness to serve as a lab rat in pursuit of automotive automation, you can buy a kit from Comma to retrofit your grocery getter with autonomous-driving ready sensors and cameras. With all the attention that Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system and Waymo’s robotaxis get, these DIY options have largely flown under the radar. We may have recently gotten a taste, however, of what the reaction to this aftermarket tech going mainstream might look like. Over the weekend, a man going by Mike LaBarbera on X posted a video of his Tesla Model Y driving itself using Comma Four, the latest version of Comma AI’s self-driving hardware. “My FSD subscription ended last January, and this isn’t Tesla Autopilot,” LaBarbera said. With this open source alternative, he boasted, he was “no longer renting a closed system.” Actually, LaBarbera clarified, what was running the car in the video is “Sunnypilot,” an Openpilot fork — someone else’s custom version of the software, essentially. While a compelling testament to how far self-driving tech has come along, the video has also alarmed some observers with how easy it apparently is to install custom tech to control your car. “I do not think we should be letting people run any software they want on their self-driving car,” said Cairo Smith, a writer, in a post that attracted more likes than the original. “It is not Skyrim for Linux. candidates.title: Scientists Alarmed by “Kelvin Wave” That Could Raise California Ocean Level by a Whole Foot
candidates.raw_excerpt: There’s a massive wave heading across the ocean straight for the California coast — not a freak tsunami, but a slow-moving surge driven by what may be one of the strongest El Niño oscillations in nearly a millennium. The phenomenon is called a “Kelvin wave,” an incomprehensibly vast displacement of warm ocean water creeping from the west Pacific toward the Americas. As the Guardian notes , the wave spans thousands of miles of surf, which is currently creeping upward toward the California coast after a slow-motion crash into South and Central America. When the full force of the wave reaches the Golden State, it could raise coastal sea levels by as much as a foot, ocean scientists told the Guardian . And due to the forces of El Niño, sea levels could remain in that elevated state for months, accelerating coastal erosion and feeding severe storms. “It’s a wave unlike the ones you’re used to at the beach,” research oceanographer at the Southwest Fisheries Science Center Mike Jacox told the Guardian . “They don’t crash, you can’t really seem them come by. This winter, we’re supposed to have some really high tides around Thanksgiving and Christmas. If you also have more storms, then you have storm surge. It’s just like you’re raising the floor on all that stuff that happens.” The wave is already swelling off the coasts of countries near the equator like Columbia and Panama. In Ecuador, data collected by the Escuela Superior Politécnica del Litoral, a public university which plays a key role in global monitoring of El Niño oscillations, found that ambient sea levels were nearly 15 inches higher than average. During periods of high tide, the surf rose to nearly 17 inches above usual levels, El Universo reported . The Kelvin wave is kicked off by unseasonably warm water temperatures in the Pacific, up to 13.5 degrees Fahrenheit higher than usual. candidates.title: SpaceX’s Troubled Starship Test Yesterday Is Looking Ominous for NASA’s Moon Landing
candidates.raw_excerpt: On its 14th flight test Monday, SpaceX’s Starship successfully flew into orbit for the first time, marking a huge milestone for the Elon Musk owned company. But it didn’t stay up there long. Originally scheduled to fly around the planet six times in a mission lasting a total of ten hours, the rocket instead returned to Earth just three hours into its orbital adventure because of an engine failure. Belly-flopping on its way down, the spaceship righted itself before making a less-than-soft landing in the Pacific, exploding in a fireball moments after touchdown. While the causes of this propulsion malfunction aren’t clear yet, experts fear that it may portend a fundamental issue with the rocket’s design, which could set back NASA’s 2028 mission, Artemis IV, in its efforts to land humans on the Moon for the first time in over half a century using the spacecraft. The launch from SpaceX’s Starbase facility in Texas on Monday achieved most of the rocket company’s objectives, including a successful first foray into orbit. While up there, the spacecraft’s upper stage deployed a payload of 26 functioning next-gen Starlink satellites (previous tests used dummies), while its lower stage booster made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico. Bringing cargo to orbit is an essential part of any practical rocket’s capabilities, making this an unimpeachable milestone. But it’s a feat that comes years behind schedule; Musk originally promised that Starship would achieve satellite deployments by 2023. A lagging schedule may continue to haunt its development. Two of the 33 Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster failed during its flight: one on the way up, and one on the way down. And one engine failed on the Starship upper stage during its ascent, forcing the remaining engines to work harder. candidates.title: OpenAI Cancels Upcoming AI Model When It Shows Signs of Being Evil

The news once again highlighted rising concerns over the AI industry losing the ability to keep their own technology in check. Now, the Sam Altman-led company is canceling the release of its next-generation AI model GPT-6.1 Astra, as the Wall Street Journal reports . OpenAI researchers found it scored poorly on alignment tests, which are designed to measure how willing a given AI model is to stick to its human overlord’s instructions. In common parlance, you could say the model was showing too many signs of being evil. The researchers found that the AI was even more willing to deceive users than previous models. It also was willing to venture far beyond the scope of its intended task without permission, per the WSJ , making use of external tools without authorization. “For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade off,” OpenAI’s head of safety systems Saachi Jain told the newspaper. “You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction.” The timing of the news is unfortunate for the company. OpenAI is kicking off its developer conference in San Francisco today, an event that’s usually reserved for the launch of new models. But now that most frontier AI labs agree to slow down the development of their models, the company is operating in a notably different environment. Meanwhile, OpenAI has promised to beef up its defenses and implement stronger guardrails for its cybersecurity testing after its AI agents have repeatedly broken out of their sandbox environments. candidates.title: Scientists Unveil Underwater Solar Panels
candidates.raw_excerpt: China’s green energy boom has seen solar panels plastered on the side of rainy mountains, on floating coastal platforms, and above bustling highways — and now, they’re even generating energy underwater. According to EuroNews , scientists working near Weizhou Island on China’s southwestern coast successfully generated electricity from sunlight at a depth of 10 meters, or nearly 33 feet, a new record for photovoltaic research. Their study, published in the research journal Joule , outlines a new type of solar panel built with perovskites — a calcium titanium oxide mineral — instead of silicon. By using pervoskite-based cells, the researchers were able to adjust the solar panels to capitalize on the kinds of blue and green sunlight waves that can penetrate the ocean’s surface. According to the paper, the peak power conversion efficiency — a measure of how much sunlight hitting a panel is converted into usable energy — reached a high of nearly 35 percent. If true, that figure puts the panels in-line with recent breakthrough research in solar cell efficiency, and a notch above the long-established Shockley-Queisser limit , a theoretical cap which limited photovoltaic efficiency to about 33 percent. Granted, the results were obtained under simulation conditions, so more rigorous testing is needed to confirm whether similar results are possible in a real-world setting. Overall, the test ran for just two hours, generating 324 milliwatt-hours, enough to power a small LED light for a few hours. Still, even sniffing the Shockley-Queisser limit with solar panels some 30 feet underwater is a noteworthy accomplishment. And as EuroNews observes, even the decidedly small amount of electricity produced far surpassed researchers’ expectations. candidates.title: CNES Publishes Call for New Rocket Launch Tracking Turrets for French Guiana
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: CSG The French space agency CNES has issued a call for new automated optical tracking systems for the Guiana Space Centre. The new system will need to be capable of tracking launch vehicles to altitudes of up to an altitude of 100 kilometres. Published on 24 September , the initiative aims to replace aging and partially obsolete equipment currently used to capture imagery of Ariane and Vega launches. CNES said the existing systems are ageing and partially obsolete. The agency wants to replace the manual and semi-automated systems with a fully automated alternative, with tracking tied directly to launch vehicle trajectory data. Beyond launch imagery for public broadcasts, the spaceport’s flight-safety teams use these systems for technical analysis and diagnostics to support post-launch investigations. The new tracking turrets will carry sensors operating in both the visible and infrared spectrum, together with very-long-focal-length optics capable of clearly observing a launch vehicle at an altitude of 100 kilometres. In total, CNES plans to procure three turrets. Two will be fixed systems, while the third will be a mobile unit that can be positioned where it’s needed. CNES will install one fixed turret on Île Royale, an island off the coast of French Guiana, and the second on the mainland. The turrets will be managed remotely and operated from a single console at the Image Production Centre (Centre de Production d’Images) in the Jupiter 2 building, which is also home to the spaceport’s main control centre. CNES expects to award the contract in the third quarter of 2027. The contract, covering the supply, installation and qualification of the new systems, is expected to run for approximately three years. candidates.title: Creative Industries Have Been Eviscerated by AI, Data Shows
candidates.raw_excerpt: If you work in a creative industry or media, you probably don’t need anybody to tell you how bad things have gotten. Still, even the most intimate first-hand knowledge can’t prepare you for the sheer scope of the devastation. As data journalist Joseph Politano found in a new Substack post , the US has lost more than 200,000 jobs in “creative” industries over the past four years — the period since the first version of ChatGPT became available to the public — with almost 50,000 of those losses coming in the last year alone. The data comes from the US Bureau of Labor statistics, the trustworthiness of which has been repeatedly undermined since Donald Trump’s return to office. Still, it remains one of the most robust and widely-used indicators of macroeconomic job data, for analysts trying to make sense of the increasingly bleak job market . “That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” Politano observes, “with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008.” Politano notes the steepest losses came in digital arts like graphic design, broadcasting, publishing, as well as films and sound recording. Though some sections of the live arts sector have actually grown precipitously — museum work and performing arts, to be precise — other types of live arts jobs, like “employment to an independent artist” have plummeted compared to years past. As a whole, job growth in media and creative industries has remained negative since 2023, as tools like generative AI — shoddy as they still are — provide an easily accessible alternative to human design, video, literary, and audio work. Though it’s never been easy to secure consistent employment in these industries, the rise of AI and the general decay of the labor economy has clearly made it harder than ever before, and the losses show little sign of stopping anytime soon. On all of Starship's previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth's gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did. What's more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company's newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket's cargo bay. Starship is a two-stage vehicle and although it’s the second stage that’s named Starship, the word is often used to refer to the entire vehicle. The first stage is Super Heavy or “Booster.” Booster lost one of its 33 engines shortly after liftoff, but that didn’t affect its performance. SpaceX did not attempt a “catch” back at the launch tower — they haven’t tried that since IFT-8 — and Booster made a soft landing in the Gulf. Starship, or “Ship,” lost one of its three RVAC (Raptor Vacuum) engines during ascent as can be seen in the image in the lower right corner. candidates.raw_excerpt: Venus is often called the Earth’s “ evil twin ” since they’re roughly the same size, formed in the same inner part of the solar system, and happen to be neighbors as well — although, as suggested by that moniker, Venus is horrendously inhospitable to life as we know it compared to our home planet. The similarities may run even deeper than previously known. Scientists have previously suggested that Venus once had a moon orbiting it, which met its demise when an enormous object impacted with it. Other researchers believe its current lack of moons — beyond several trojan asteroids that don’t directly orbit the planet and therefore don’t meet the definition of a moon — means that Venus never experienced the kind of impact that could’ve dislodged enough material to form a natural satellite. Now, a new study published in The Astrophysical Journal upends that consensus, with the authors suggesting that Venus did indeed once have a moon — until it spiraled inwards and crashed into the planet’s surface in an apocalyptic demise. Put simply, Venus may have devoured its own moon. “My study shows Venus didn’t require a catastrophe to arrive at what we can see today,” said lead author and University of California, Riverside, astrophysicist Stephen Kane in a statement . “It turns out the gravity of the planet itself combined with the rate at which it spins naturally caused the moon to collapse on top of it.” The findings could have significant implications, even when it comes to investigating the habitability of distant worlds. “When people think about Earth twins around other stars, one question they ask is, ‘Does it have a moon?'” Kane said. “”My study shows a disturbing scenario for many of those cases. candidates.raw_excerpt: While a rising majority of workers in the take a negative attitude toward AI in the workplace, others are welcoming the tech with open arms — even going so far as to pay for AI services out of their own pockets. So dexterous is our disembodied perambulator that it can navigate multiple surfaces and even clack away at a keyboard while supporting its own weight, footage of its exploits shows. It’s kind of adorable when you watch it in action, like as it plays a game on a computer. But there’s a somewhat creepy, arachnid quality to its twitchy gait — and it’s also, perhaps, reminiscent of a sci-fi horror film’s killer robot that refuses to die even when its body is destroyed. (See also: metamachines .) Besides haunting a final girl from the grave, an autonomous hand could have some practical applications, the researchers say. “A robotic hand with its own mobility could operate in confined workspaces without requiring the arm that normally carries it to follow,” the researchers wrote in a new paper about their work. “For example, a larger robot could place the hand on a support surface near a restricted opening. Adding to the difficulty is that, because the hand is designed to be human-like, the fingers are unequal lengths.
